q: Which is the strength of an array and the weakness of a linked list?
options: Reading item number i in one step
Adding at the front in one step
Never needing memory
Keeping items sorted
why: An array can jump to index i: O(1). A linked list must follow the arrows from the head: O(i).

q: In JavaScript, what is slow about `arr.shift()` on a big array?
options: It also copies the whole array to a new place
Every other item moves one place, so it is O(n) per call
It throws an error when the array is empty
It sorts the array first
why: 200,000 shifts took about 4,597 ms; a queue with a head index took about 5 ms. Small arrays look fine, big ones do not.

q: When you reverse a linked list, why do you save `curr.next` before changing it?
options: JavaScript requires it
To keep the list sorted
The only way to reach the rest of the list is through `curr.next`
To make the code shorter
why: Flip the arrow first and nothing points to the rest of the list any more. Save next, flip the arrow, move both pointers forward.

q: How do the slow and fast pointers find a cycle in a linked list?
options: Both move 1 step and we count the nodes
Fast goes to the end and back
They compare the values of the nodes
Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps, and they meet only if there is a loop
why: Inside a loop the fast pointer gains one step on the slow one each turn, so they must meet. It costs O(n) time and O(1) space.

q: Which problem is a natural fit for a stack?
options: Checking that brackets are matched in the right order
Serving customers in the order they arrived
Looking up a user by id
Finding the middle of a sorted list
why: A stack gives back the newest item first. The last bracket opened must be the first one closed.

q: `isValid('((')` returns false. Which line catches it?
options: `if (!pairs[ch]) stack.push(ch)`
`return stack.length === 0`
`const stack = []`
`for (const ch of s)`
why: Both characters are openers, so nothing fails in the loop. The last line catches brackets that were opened and never closed.
